summary.text: Define \(b_0=-2\), \(b_1=56\), and \(b_{n+2}=4b_{n+1}-64b_n\); algebra shows that both \(a(2n+1)\) and \(b_n^2\) satisfy the recurrence \(x_{n+3}=-48x_{n+2}+3072x_{n+1}+262144x_n\). Their first three values agree, so induction gives \(a(2n+1)=b_n^2\) for every \(n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(r\ge 0\),
\[
a_{r+4}=-4a_{r+3}+256a_{r+1}+4096a_r.
\]
We prove that every odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is a square.

Introduce an auxiliary integer sequence \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
b_0=-2,\qquad b_1=56,
\]
and
\[
b_{n+2}=4b_{n+1}-64b_n\qquad(n\ge 0).
\]
We will prove the stronger identity
\[
\boxed{a_{2n+1}=b_n^2}
\]
for every \(n\ge 0\).

First we derive a recurrence involving every other term of \(a\). We claim that, for every \(k\ge 0\),
\[
\boxed{a_{k+6}=-48a_{k+4}+3072a_{k+2}+262144a_k.}\tag{1}
\]
Indeed, three successive instances of the defining recurrence are
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k+4}&=-4a_{k+3}+256a_{k+1}+4096a_k,\\
a_{k+5}&=-4a_{k+4}+256a_{k+2}+4096a_{k+1},\\
a_{k+6}&=-4a_{k+5}+256a_{k+3}+4096a_{k+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting the expression for \(a_{k+5}\) into the last equation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k+6}
&=-4\bigl(-4a_{k+4}+256a_{k+2}+4096a_{k+1}\bigr)
  +256a_{k+3}+4096a_{k+2}\\
&=16a_{k+4}+3072a_{k+2}+256a_{k+3}-16384a_{k+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand, multiplying the first displayed recurrence by \(-64\) yields
\[
-64a_{k+4}=256a_{k+3}-16384a_{k+1}-262144a_k,
\]
so
\[
256a_{k+3}-16384a_{k+1}=-64a_{k+4}+262144a_k.
\]
Substitution into the preceding expression for \(a_{k+6}\) proves (1):
\[
a_{k+6}
=(16-64)a_{k+4}+3072a_{k+2}+262144a_k
=-48a_{k+4}+3072a_{k+2}+262144a_k.
\]
Thus, in particular, the odd-indexed subsequence of \(a\) satisfies a third-order recurrence.

Next we show that the squares of the terms of \(b\) satisfy the same recurrence. We claim that for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
\boxed{b_{n+3}^2=-48b_{n+2}^2+3072b_{n+1}^2+262144b_n^2.}\tag{2}
\]
To see this, write \(x=b_n\) and \(y=b_{n+1}\). The recurrence for \(b\) gives
\[
b_{n+2}=4y-64x,
\]
and then
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+3}
&=4b_{n+2}-64b_{n+1}\\
&=4(4y-64x)-64y\\
&=-48y-256x.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+3}^2
&=(-48y-256x)^2\\
&=2304y^2+24576xy+65536x^2.
\end{aligned}\tag{3}
\]
Meanwhile,
\[
\begin{aligned}
-48b_{n+2}^2+3072b_{n+1}^2+262144b_n^2
&=-48(4y-64x)^2+3072y^2+262144x^2\\
&=-48(16y^2-512xy+4096x^2)
  +3072y^2+262144x^2\\
&=2304y^2+24576xy+65536x^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
This agrees with (3), proving (2).

We now establish \(a_{2n+1}=b_n^2\) by strong induction on \(n\). Three initial cases are needed because (1) and (2) are third-order recurrences.

For \(n=0\),
\[
a_{2\cdot 0+1}=a_1=4=(-2)^2=b_0^2.
\]
For \(n=1\),
\[
a_{2\cdot 1+1}=a_3=3136=56^2=b_1^2.
\]
For \(n=2\), first the recurrence for \(b\) gives
\[
b_2=4b_1-64b_0=4\cdot56-64(-2)=224+128=352.
\]
To compute the corresponding term of \(a\), we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_4
&=-4a_3+256a_1+4096a_0\\
&=-4\cdot3136+256\cdot4+4096(-1)\\
&=-15616,
\end{aligned}
\]
and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_5
&=-4a_4+256a_2+4096a_1\\
&=-4(-15616)+256\cdot176+4096\cdot4\\
&=62464+45056+16384\\
&=123904.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since
\[
352^2=123904,
\]
it follows that
\[
a_{2\cdot2+1}=a_5=b_2^2.
\]

Now let \(m\ge 0\), and suppose the desired identity is already known for the three indices \(m,m+1,m+2\); in a strong induction these are all smaller than \(m+3\). Thus
\[
a_{2m+1}=b_m^2,
\qquad
a_{2m+3}=b_{m+1}^2,
\qquad
a_{2m+5}=b_{m+2}^2.
\]
Apply (1) with \(k=2m+1\). Since
\[
(2m+1)+2=2m+3,
\quad
(2m+1)+4=2m+5,
\quad
(2m+1)+6=2m+7=2(m+3)+1,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2(m+3)+1}
&=a_{2m+7}\\
&=-48a_{2m+5}+3072a_{2m+3}+262144a_{2m+1}\\
&=-48b_{m+2}^2+3072b_{m+1}^2+262144b_m^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
By (2), the last expression is exactly \(b_{m+3}^2\). Therefore
\[
a_{2(m+3)+1}=b_{m+3}^2,
\]
which completes the induction.

Hence, for every nonnegative integer \(n\),
\[
a_{2n+1}=b_n^2.
\]
Because \(b_n\) is an integer, this exhibits \(a_{2n+1}\) as a perfect square for every \(n\ge 0\), as required.
